Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 1–2:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat as-Sajdah. It is Meccan, except for three verses revealed at Medina, which are His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was defiantly disobedient?﴾ [As-Sajdah: 18], the three verses being complete. This was said by al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Others said: except for five verses, from His, the Exalted, saying: "Their sides forsake their beds" [[See vol. 15, p. 3 onward.]] up to His saying: ﴿the punishment of the Fire, which you used to deny﴾ [As-Sajdah: 20–16]. The surah has thirty verses. It was also said twenty-nine.

In the Sahih, from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the Fajr prayer on Friday "Alif. Lam. Mim. The revelation" (as-Sajdah) and "Has there come upon man a period of time" (al-Insan), the hadith. Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his Musnad from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would not sleep until he had recited "Alif. Lam. Mim. The revelation" (as-Sajdah) and ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾ [Al-Mulk: 1].

Al-Darimi said: Abu al-Mughirah informed us, saying: Abdah related to us from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, who said: Recite al-Munjiyah, which is "Alif. Lam. Mim. The revelation," for it has reached me that a man used to recite it and nothing else, and he was greatly sinful, so it spread its wing over him and said: "My Lord, forgive him, for he used to recite me often." So the Lord interceded for him and said: "Write for him a good deed for every sin, and raise him a degree."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif. Lam. Mim. (1) The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds. (2)

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. The revelation of the Book﴾. There is consensus on the raising (rafa') of "tanzil al-kitab" (the revelation of the Book). Had it been in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), it would have been permissible, as the Kufans recited: ﴿Indeed you are among the messengers. On a straight path. A revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 3–5]. "Tanzil" is raised as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "la rayba fihi" (there is no doubt in it). Or it is a predicate with an omitted subject, i.e., this is the revelation, or the recited is the revelation, or these letters are the revelation. "Alif. Lam. Mim" indicates the mention of the letters. It is also permissible that "la rayba fihi" be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-kitab," and "min rabb al-alamin" be the predicate. Makki said: this is the best of them. The meaning of "in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds" is: there is no doubt that it is from Allah; it is not sorcery, nor poetry, nor soothsaying, nor the fables of the ancients.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 3:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ This "am" is the disjunctive "am" (am al-munqati'ah), which is estimated to be equivalent to "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative alif, meaning: "Rather, do they say...?" It indicates a shift from one topic to another. Indeed, He, mighty and majestic, had affirmed that it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, and that there is no doubt about it. Then He turned away from that to His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾, i.e., He has fabricated it and forged it.

(﴿Rather, it is the truth from your Lord﴾) He denied their claim of fabrication. (﴿So that you may warn a people﴾) Qatadah said: It means the Quraysh, who were an unlettered people, and to whom no warner had come before Muhammad (ﷺ). The phrase ﴿so that you may warn﴾ is connected to what precedes it, so one does not stop at ﴿from your Lord﴾. It is also permissible for it to be connected to an implied element, the estimate being: "He sent it down so that you may warn a people," in which case it is permissible to stop at ﴿from your Lord﴾. As for "ma" in His saying ﴿who had not come to them﴾, it is a negation. ﴿A warner﴾ is a relative clause (silah). And "nadhir" (warner) is in the nominative position, and it means the one who gives notice and instills fear. It has also been said: the intended "people" are the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah) between Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both; this was said by Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. It has also been said: the proof was established for them by God, mighty and majestic, through the warning of earlier messengers, even though they had not seen a messenger, and this meaning has already been mentioned [[See vol. 6, p. 121.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 4:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is Allah who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days﴾. He made them aware of the perfection of His power so that they would hear the Qur'an and reflect upon it. The meaning of "created" (khalaqa) is that He originated and brought into existence after non-existence, after they were not anything. "In six days" means from Sunday to the end of Friday. Al-Hasan said: from the days of this world (al-dunya). Ibn Abbas said: the day among the six days in which Allah created the heavens and the earth is equal to a thousand years of the years of this world. Al-Dahhak said: "in six thousand years," that is, within the span of six days of the days of the Hereafter.

(Then He established Himself upon the Throne) This has been discussed previously in al-A'raf and al-Baqarah [[See vol. 7 p. 219 and vol. 1 p. 254.]] and elsewhere, and we have mentioned what the scholars say about it in full in (al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna) (The Most Beautiful Names of Allah explained). "Thumma" (then) here is not for sequence; rather, it carries the meaning of "wa" (and).

(You have no protector or intercessor besides Him) That is, the disbelievers have no protector who prevents their punishment, nor any intercessor. It is permissible to read "wali" and "shafi'" in the nominative case (raf') according to their position (mahall).

(Will you not then remember?) Regarding His power and His creation.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 32, verse 5:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He directs the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He sends down the decree (al-qada') and the divine measure (al-qadar). It was also said: He sends down the revelation (al-wahy) with Jibril. Amr ibn Murra narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, who said: Four angels direct the affairs of the world: Jibril, Mikail, the Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt), and Israfil, may the blessings of Allah be upon them all. As for Jibril, he is entrusted with the winds and the hosts. As for Mikail, he is entrusted with the rain and the water. As for the Angel of Death, he is entrusted with seizing the souls. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them. It has been said that the Throne (al-Arsh) is the place of direction (al-tadbir), just as what is below the Throne is the place of detailing (al-tafsil). Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne and subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term. He directs the affair, detailing the signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. And what is below the heavens is the place of turning and variation (al-tasrif). Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And We have certainly varied it among them that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 50].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then it ascends to Him﴾. Yahya ibn Sallam said: It is Jibril, who ascends to the heaven after descending with the revelation. Al-Naqqash said: It is the angel who directs the affair from the heaven to the earth. It was also said: It refers to the reports of the people of the earth, which ascend to Him with the angels who carry them, as stated by Ibn Shajara.

(...in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count.) It was also said: "Then it ascends to Him" means that this affair and direction return to Him after the end of the world, "in a day whose measure is a thousand years," and that is the Day of Resurrection. According to the preceding opinions, the pronoun in "ya'ruju" (it ascends) refers to the angel, and he was not mentioned explicitly because he is understood from the meaning. It has come explicitly in His saying in "Sa'ala sa'il": ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. The pronoun in "ilayhi" (to Him) refers either to the heaven, according to the dialect of those who make it masculine, or to the place of the angel to which he returns, or to the name of Allah, may He be exalted, and what is meant is the place where He has established it. When it returns to Allah, it has returned to the heaven, that is, to Sidrat al-Muntaha, for to it rises whatever ascends from the earth, and from it descends whatever is sent down to it. The meaning of this is established in Sahih Muslim.

The pronoun in "miqdaruhu" (its measure) refers to the direction. The meaning is: the measure of that direction is a thousand years of the years of the world, that is, He decides the affair of each thing for a thousand years within one day, then He conveys it to His angels. When that period has passed, He decides for another thousand years, and so on forever. This was said by Mujahid. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the ascent. It was also said: the meaning is that He directs the affairs of the world until the Hour arrives, then that affair ascends to Him and He judges it in a day whose measure is a thousand years. It was also said: the meaning is that He directs the affair of the sun in its rising, its setting, and its return to its place of rising, in a day whose measure in distance is a thousand years. Ibn Abbas said: The meaning is that its measure, if other than the angel traveled it, would be a thousand years, because the descent is five hundred years and the ascent five hundred years. This was narrated from a group of the exegetes, and it is the choice of al-Tabari, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi. It is also the meaning of the first opinion, namely that Jibril, because of the speed of his journey, covers a distance of a thousand years in one of your days, as mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. Al-Mawardi mentioned from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak that the angel ascends in a day whose distance is a thousand years. From Qatada it is narrated that the angel descends and ascends in a day whose measure is a thousand years, so the measure of his descent is five hundred years and the measure of his ascent five hundred years, according to the view of Qatada and al-Suddi. According to the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, the descent is a thousand years and the ascent a thousand years.

"Mimma ta'uddun" (of what you count) means: of what you reckon from the days of the world. This day is an expression for a period measured as a thousand years of the years of the world, and it is not a day that fills a daytime between two nights, because that is not the case with Allah. The Arabs sometimes express the duration of an era by a day, as the poet said:

*Two days: a day of halts and gatherings,*
*and a day of marching toward the enemies, a journey through the whole day (ta'wib).*

He does not mean two specific days; rather, he meant that their time is divided into two halves, and he expressed each of the two halves by a day. Ibn Abi Abla read "ya'ruju" in the passive voice. It was also read "ya'uddun" with the letter ya'. As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In a day whose measure was fifty thousand years﴾, it is problematic alongside this verse. Abdullah ibn Fayruz al-Daylami asked Abdullah ibn Abbas about this verse and about His saying: "in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years." He said: "They are days which He named, may He be glorified, and I do not know what they are, so I dislike to say about them what I do not know." Then Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab was asked about them and said: "I do not know." I informed him of the saying of Ibn Abbas, and Ibn al-Musayyab said to the questioner: "This is Ibn Abbas, who refrained from speaking about them, and he is more knowledgeable than I am." Then the scholars discussed this, and it was said: the verse ﴿A questioner asked﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1] refers to the Day of Resurrection, unlike this verse. The meaning is that Allah made it, in its hardship for the disbelievers, like fifty thousand years, as said by Ibn Abbas. The Arabs describe the days of hardship as long and the days of joy as short. The poet said:

*And a day like the shadow of a spear, its length shortened by the blood of the wineskin (wine) for us and the clapping of the lutes.*

It was also said: the Day of Resurrection has days in it, some of which measure a thousand years and some of which measure fifty thousand years. It was also said: the times of the Resurrection vary, so the disbeliever is punished with one kind of punishment for a thousand years, then he moves to another kind whose duration is fifty thousand years. It was also said: the stations of the Resurrection are fifty stations, each station a thousand years. So the meaning of "it ascends to Him in a day whose measure is a thousand years" is: the measure of a time or a station of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Nahhas said: "Yawm" (day) in the language means "time," so the meaning is: the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a time whose measure was a thousand years, and in another time whose measure was fifty thousand years. It was narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih concerning "in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years" that he said: it is the distance between the lowest part of the earth and the Throne. Al-Tha'labi mentioned from Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Dahhak concerning His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4], that what is meant is from the earth to Sidrat al-Muntaha, where Jibril is. The verse says: Jibril and the angels with him from among the people of his station travel a distance of fifty thousand years in one day of the days of the world. His saying "ilayhi" (to Him) means to the place to which Allah commanded them to ascend. This is like the saying of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], meaning the land of Sham. And He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 100], meaning to Madinah.

Abu Hurayra said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "An angel from my Lord, mighty and majestic, came to me with a message, then he raised one foot and placed it above the heaven, and the other on the earth, and had not yet lifted it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, meaning: He knows what is hidden from the creation and what is present to them. "That" (dhalika) is in the sense of "I" (ana), as its explanation has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 157 onward.]]. The statement also carries the sense of threat and warning, meaning: make your deeds and your words sincere, for I will recompense you for them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 7–9:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Who made everything He created good﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "khalqahu" (خَلْقَهُ) with the lam sukun. The rest read it with a fatha on the lam. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred it, seeking its ease. It is a past-tense verb in the position of a descriptive adjective (na't) for "shay'" (thing). The meaning, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "He perfected everything He created", that is, He brought it into being as He willed, and it did not deviate from His will. Another view: everything He created is good, because no one can bring forth its like, and it points to its Creator. As for the one who reads it with a sukun on the lam, according to Sibawayh it is a verbal noun (masdar), because His saying "made good everything He created" indicates "He created everything with a creation", so it is like ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾ [an-Naml: 88] and ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾ [an-Nisa': 24]. According to others it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "kull" (every), meaning: the One who made good the creation of everything. It is a second object according to some grammarians, on the basis that the meaning of "ahsana" is "made understand and made know", so it takes two objects, meaning: He made everything He created understood. It was also said: it is in the accusative as an explanatory specification (tafsir), and the meaning is: He made every thing good in creation. It was also said: it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, and the meaning is: He made every thing good in its creation. Its meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and "ahsana" means "perfected and made firm", so He is good in respect of the purposes for which it was intended. From this meaning, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: the buttocks of the monkey are not beautiful, but they are perfected and firm. Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid regarding "who made everything He created good" that he said: "He perfected it." This is like His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], meaning He did not create man in the form of beasts, nor did He create beasts in the form of man. It is permissible to read "khalquhu" (خَلْقُهُ) with a damma, on the estimation "that is its creation". It was also said: it is general in wording but specific in meaning, and the meaning is: the goodness of the creation of every good thing. It was also said: it is general in both wording and meaning, that is, He made everything He created good, to the extent that He made the dog good in its creation, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: in the buttocks of the monkey there is beauty.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾, meaning Adam.

(Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, despised.) This has been discussed in "al-Mu'minun" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: "min ma'in mahin" (from a despised fluid) is weak.

Others said: "mahin" means it has no value in the eyes of people.

(Then He proportioned him) this returns to Adam, that is, He proportioned his creation, (and breathed into him of His spirit). Then He returned to his descendants and said: ﴿and made for you hearing and sight﴾. It was also said: then He made that despised water into a balanced creation, and placed the spirit within it, and attributed it to Himself in honour. Also, it is from His action and creation, just as He attributed the servant to Himself by His saying "My servant". He expressed it with "breathing" because the spirit is of the genus of wind. This has already been explained in detail in "an-Nisa'" and elsewhere.

(Little is it that you give thanks.) That is: then you do not give thanks, but rather you disbelieve.

This is like His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], meaning He did not create man in the form of beasts, nor did He create beasts in the form of man. It is permissible to read "khalquhu" (خَلْقُهُ) with a damma, on the estimation "that is its creation". It was also said: it is general in wording but specific in meaning, and the meaning is: the goodness of the creation of every good thing. It was also said: it is general in both wording and meaning, that is, He made everything He created good, to the extent that He made the dog good in its creation, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: in the buttocks of the monkey there is beauty.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He began the creation of man from clay﴾, meaning Adam.

(Then He made his offspring from an extract of a liquid, despised.) This has been discussed in "al-Mu'minun" and elsewhere. Al-Zajjaj said: "min ma'in mahin" (from a despised fluid) is weak.

Others said: "mahin" means it has no value in the eyes of people.

(Then He proportioned him) this returns to Adam, that is, He proportioned his creation, (and breathed into him of His spirit). Then He returned to his descendants and said: ﴿and made for you hearing and sight﴾. It was also said: then He made that despised water into a balanced creation, and placed the spirit within it, and attributed it to Himself in honour. Also, it is from His action and creation, just as He attributed the servant to Himself by His saying "My servant". He expressed it with "breathing" because the spirit is of the genus of wind. This has already been explained in detail in "an-Nisa'" and elsewhere.

(Little is it that you give thanks.) That is: then you do not give thanks, but rather you disbelieve.

This is the saying of those who deny the resurrection, meaning: we have perished, we have been annihilated, and we have become dust. Its root comes from the Arab saying: "the water went astray (ḍalla) in the milk," when it disappears. The Arabs also say of a thing that has been overcome by something else until its trace is hidden in it: "it has gone astray (ḍalla)." Al-Akhtal said:

*You were the speck in a turbid, foaming sea,*
*which the flood cast up, and so it went astray in utter straying.*

Qutrub said: the meaning of "ḍallalnā" is "we became absent in the earth." He recited the verse of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

*So those who lost him returned with a clear sign,*
*and there were left behind at al-Jawlan resolve and gain.*

Ibn Muhaysin and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read *ḍalilnā* with a kasra on the lam, and this is a dialect form. Al-Jawhari said: "I have strayed (ḍalaltu), I stray (aḍillu)." God the Exalted says: ﴿Say: If I stray, I stray only to my own detriment﴾ [Saba': 50][[See p. 313 of this part.]]. This is the dialect of Najd, and it is the eloquent form. The people of al-'Aliyah say *ḍalilt* with a kasra on the lam, *aḍill*, and he is *ḍāll* and *tall*; the noun is *ḍalāla* and *talāla*. *Aḍallahu* means he lost it or destroyed it. It is said: "the dead was lost (uḍilla)" when he was buried. He said:

*So those who lost him returned...*

[the verse above].

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "aḍlaltu ba'īrī" means my camel went away from you. "Ḍallaltu al-masjida wa al-dār" means I did not know the place of the mosque or the house, and likewise every fixed thing that cannot be found by guidance. In the hadith: "Perhaps I will lose God (la'allī aḍillu Allāh)," meaning I will lose Him, that is, He will be hidden from him, from the saying of God the Exalted: "When we have strayed (ḍalalnā) in the earth," that is, when we have been hidden. "Allah led him astray (aḍallahu Allāh), so he strayed." You say: "You guide the one who has strayed, but you cannot guide the one who has made himself stray."

Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read *ṣalalnā* with a ṣād, meaning "we became rotten." This is the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (raḍiya Allāhu 'anhu). Al-Nahhas said: "*ṣalalnā* is not known in the language, but it is said: *ṣalla al-laḥm* and *aṣalla*, and *khamma* and *akhamma*, when the meat became rotten." Al-Jawhari said: "*ṣalla al-laḥm* yaṣillu, with a kasra, *ṣulūlan*, meaning it became rotten, whether cooked or raw." Al-Hutay'a said:

*That is a youth who gives away his pot's portion;*
*the rotten meat does not spoil for him.*

*Aṣalla* is similar to it.

"Are we indeed (innā) in a new creation?" meaning: will we be created anew after that? It is also read *a'innā* (with interrogation). Al-Nahhas said: Here is a difficult question of Arabic grammar: what governs *idhā* (when)? *Inna* does not govern what follows it on what precedes it, and the question is harder with the interrogative, since what follows the interrogative is more fitting not to be governed by what precedes it from *inna*; how then when both are combined? The answer on the reading of whoever reads *innā* is that the governing word is *ḍalalnā*, and on the reading of whoever reads *a'innā*, the governing word is a hidden verb, and the estimate is: "Will we be raised when we have died?" There is also another question: where is the answer to *idhā* on the first reading, since it carries the meaning of a condition? The answer is that after it is a past verb, and for that reason this is permitted.

﴿Nay, they are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾. That is, it is not that they deny God's power to restore, since they acknowledge His power; rather, they believed that there is no reckoning for them, and that they will not meet God the Exalted.

There are two issues here.

The first concerns God's words: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death who has been charged with you will take your souls﴾. When He mentioned their denial of resurrection, He mentioned their dying and that He would bring them back. "Yatawaffakum" comes from tawaffa the number or the thing, meaning to complete it and take all of it. It is said: "Allah tawaffahu," meaning He completed his soul and took it. And "tawaffaytu mali min fulan" means "I received my full due from so-and-so." The "Angel of Death" is named Azra'il, and his name means "servant of Allah," as was mentioned in al-Baqarah [See vol. 2, p. 38.]. All of his actions are by the command of Allah, by His creation and His origination. It is related in a hadith that "Allah takes the souls of all animals Himself, without the Angel of Death," as if He were ending their life. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned this. I say: the opposite has also been related, that the Angel of Death takes the souls of all creatures, even the flea and the mosquito. Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the Angel of Death beside the head of a man from the Ansar, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Be gentle with my companion, for he is a believer." The Angel of Death (peace be upon him) said: "O Muhammad, be content and let your eye be comforted, for I am gentle with every believer. And know that there is no household of clay or of hair, on land or sea, that I do not inspect every day five times, so that I know their young and old better than they know themselves. By Allah, O Muhammad, if I wanted to take the soul of a mosquito I could not do so unless Allah commanded its taking." Ja'far ibn 'Ali said: It has reached me that he inspects them at the times of the prayers. Al-Mawardi mentioned this.

Al-Khatib Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn Thabit al-Baghdadi mentioned and said: Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Khallal told me, saying: Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman al-Saffar told us, saying: Abu Bakr Hamid al-Misri told us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub al-'Allaf told us, saying: Sulayman ibn Muhayr al-Kilabi told us, saying: I was in the presence of Malik ibn Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), when a man came to him and asked: "Abu 'Abd Allah, do the fleas have their souls taken by the Angel of Death?" He said: Malik lowered his head for a long time, then said: "Do they have souls?" He said: "Yes." He said: "The Angel of Death takes their souls. ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Az-Zumar: 42]." [See vol. 15, p. 260 onward.]

Ibn 'Atiyyah said after mentioning the hadith: The matter is the same with the children of Adam, except that it is a kind that is honoured by the action of an angel, with angels along with him in taking their souls. Allah created the Angel of Death and created by his hands the taking of souls, drawing them out of the bodies and bringing them out of them. Allah created an army who are with him, doing his work by His command. He said: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾ [Al-Anfal: 50], and He said: ﴿Our messengers take his soul﴾ [Al-An'am: 61]. This meaning has already passed in al-An'am [See vol. 7, p. 6 and p. 99.]. The Originator (al-Bari') is the Creator of all, the true Doer of every act. Allah said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep﴾ [Az-Zumar: 42]; ﴿He who created death and life﴾ [Al-Mulk: 2]; ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ [Al-A'raf: 158]. So the Angel of Death takes, the assistants strive, and Allah releases the spirit. This is the reconciliation between the verses and the hadiths. However, since the Angel of Death is the one who undertakes that through intermediation and direct action, the taking (tawaffi) is attributed to him, just as creation is attributed to the angel, as was mentioned in al-Hajj [See vol. 12, p. 7.]. It is related from Mujahid that the world is before the Angel of Death like a basin before a person, from which he takes whatever he wishes. This meaning has also been related as marfu' (traced back to the Prophet), and we mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkira. It is also related that when Allah entrusted the Angel of Death with taking souls, he said: "My Lord, You have made me mentioned with evil, and the children of Adam will curse me." Allah said to him: "I will make for death causes and means of illnesses and diseases, to which they will attribute death, so no one will mention you except with good." We have mentioned this fully in al-Tadhkira. We have also mentioned that he calls the souls and they come to him, and he takes them, then hands them over to the angels of mercy or of punishment, with what is a cure for whoever wishes to understand this.

The second issue: some scholars used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of wakalah (agency or delegation), from His words "wukkila bikum," meaning in the taking of souls. Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is derived from its wording, not from its meaning. If this principle were applied consistently, we would say of His words: ﴿Say: O people, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ [Al-A'raf: 158], that it is a deputyship on behalf of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, and an agency in conveying His message. We would also say of His words: ﴿And give zakat﴾ [An-Nur: 56] that it is an agency, since Allah guaranteed the provision of every creature, assigned the wealthy as the means of sustenance, and directed them that the provision of the poor is with them, and commanded that it be handed over to them in a known amount at a known time. He arranged it by His knowledge, executed it by His rule, and determined it by His wisdom. Rulings do not depend on wording unless they apply to their original subjects with their intended aims. If they appear in other than their intended purpose, they are not attached to them. Do you not see that buying and selling are known in both wording and meaning, and He said: ﴿Allah has bought from the believers their selves and their wealth, for that they will have paradise﴾ [At-Tawbah: 111]? It is not said that this verse is evidence for permitting a master to trade with his slave, because the two purposes differ. As for the claim that if there is no way other than the meanings, it is said that this verse is evidence that a judge may appoint someone to take the right from the one who owes it by force, without that person having any act of his own in that or any need for his consent when that is found."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord﴾. It is an inceptive statement (ibtida') and its predicate (khabar). Al-Zajjaj said: The address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to his community. The meaning is: If only you could see, O Muhammad, those who deny the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment, you would see a marvel. The view of Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) differs from this, and the meaning is: O Muhammad, say to the criminal: If only you could see when the criminals hang their heads before their Lord, you would feel regret for what came from you.

"Hanging their heads" means from remorse, shame, sorrow, humiliation and grief. "Before their Lord" means at the reckoning by their Lord and the recompense for their deeds. "Our Lord" means they say: ﴿Our Lord﴾. "We have seen" means: we have seen what we used to deny. "And we have heard" means what we used to reject. It is also said: "We have seen" refers to the truth of Your threat, and "we have heard" refers to the confirmation of Your messengers. They saw when sight no longer benefits them, and they heard when hearing no longer benefits them. ﴿So send us back﴾ means to the worldly life. ﴿That we may do righteousness; indeed we are certain﴾ means: we are believers in the Resurrection, as said by al-Naqqash. It is also said: we believe in what Muhammad ﷺ brought, that it is true, as said by Yahya ibn Sallam. Sufyan al-Thawri said: Allah Almighty refuted them, saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden, and indeed they are liars﴾ [see vol. 6, p. 409 and following]. It is also said: the meaning of ﴿indeed we are certain﴾ is that the doubts have now left us, and they used to hear and see in the world, but they did not reflect; they were like one who neither sees nor hears, so when they awakened in the Hereafter, they became as though they had heard and seen. It is also said: meaning, our Lord, the proof is Yours, for we have seen Your messengers and the wonders of Your creation in the world, and we have heard their speech, so we have no argument. This is their acknowledgment, then they asked to be returned to the world so that they might believe.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When they said, "Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so send us back that we may do righteousness; indeed we are certain," He answered them with His words, "And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance." He means: If I had willed, I would have guided all people, and none of them would have differed. "But the word from Me has come into effect..." up to the end of the verse. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned it in his (Raqa'iq) in a long hadith. We have mentioned it in al-Tadhkira.

Al-Nahhas said: Regarding "And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance," there are two opinions. One: that it refers to the world. The other: that the context of the speech indicates that it refers to the Hereafter, meaning: had We willed, We would have returned them to the world and the trial, as they asked. "But the word from Me has come into effect: I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together" means: the word from Me has come into effect that I will surely punish whoever disobeys Me with the Fire of Hell. Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, knew that if He returned them, they would revert, as He said, "And if they were returned, they would surely revert to what they were forbidden" (al-An'am 28). This guidance means the creation of knowledge in the heart.

The interpretation of the Mu'tazilah: "And had We willed, We would have compelled them to guidance by displaying terrifying signs," but it is not fitting for Him to do this, because it would nullify the purpose for which the obligation was imposed, namely reward, which is not deserved except through what the responsible person does by his own choice.

The Imamiyyah said in interpreting it: It is permissible that He intends their guidance to the path of Paradise in the Hereafter, and that He does not punish anyone; but the word from Him is that He will fill Hell. According to us, it is not obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, to guide all of them to it. They said: Rather, what is obligatory is the guidance of the infallible; as for one who has committed a sin, it is permissible to guide him to the Fire as a recompense for his deeds. There is an objection to the permissibility of this, since they are certain that the intended meaning is guidance to faith. The scholars have spoken against them on these two interpretations with what is sufficient in the foundations of religion. The closest answer to them is to say: It has become clear, both for us and for you, that Allah, glorified is He, does not guide them by way of compulsion, coercion and force; otherwise that would lead to the doctrine of the Jabriyyah (determinists), which is a base doctrine for us and for you. Nothing remains except that the believers who are guided were guided by Allah, exalted is He, to faith and obedience by way of choice, so that the obligation is valid. Whoever wills believes and obeys by choice, not by compulsion. Allah, exalted is He, said: "For whoever among you wills to take the straight path" (al-Takwir 28), and He said: "So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way" (al-Muzzammil 19) [see vol. 19, p. 150]. Then He followed these two verses with His saying: "And you will not will except that Allah wills" (al-Takwir 29). So the faith of the believers occurred by their will, and He negated that they will except that Allah wills. [What is between the brackets is missing from manuscripts j and k.]

For this reason, the Mujbirah (Jabriyyah) went to excess when they saw that their guidance to faith was tied to the will of Allah, and so they said: The creatures are compelled in all their obedience, taking as evidence His saying: "And you will not will except that Allah wills." And the Qadariyyah went to excess when they saw that their guidance to faith was tied to the will of the servants, so they said: The creatures are creators of their own actions, taking as evidence His saying: "For whoever among you wills to take the straight path." Our position is moderation in belief, a doctrine between the doctrines of the Jabriyyah and the Qadariyyah, and "the best of matters are their middle course." This is because the people of truth said: We distinguish between what we are compelled to and what we choose. We perceive a difference between the trembling movement that occurs in a person's hand without his effort or will and not accompanied by his power, and the movement of choice when he moves his hand in a movement similar to the trembling. Whoever does not distinguish between the two movements, the trembling movement and the movement of choice, both of which exist in his self and are perceived in his hand by his observation and the perception of his senses, is deranged in his intellect, impaired in his senses, and outside the party of the sensible. This is the clear truth, and it is a path between the paths of excess and deficiency. And:

"Both extremes of the course of affairs are blameworthy."

[This is the second half of a verse whose first half is: "Do not go to extremes in any matter, but take the middle course."]

On this basis, the scholars of speculative theology chose to call this position between the two positions "acquisition" (kasb), and they took this designation from the Mighty Book of Allah, namely His saying, glorified is He: "It has what it earned, and against it is what it has acquired" (al-Baqarah 286) [see vol. 3, p. 424].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this day of yours﴾. On this there are two views. The first is that it is from the kind of forgetting that carries no remembrance, meaning they did not act for this day, so they were like those who forget. The second is that "you forgot" (*nasītum*) means "you abandoned," and likewise "We forget you" (*innā nasīnākum*). Muḥammad ibn Yazīd argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 115]. He said: "The proof that it means abandoned is that Allah, mighty and majestic, related of Iblis that he said: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels﴾ [al-A'rāf: 20]. Had Adam been forgetful, [Iblis] would have reminded him." And he recited:

*As if it, coming out from the side of its flank, were a skewer of a drinking party, which they forgot at the place of burning.*

[The skewer (*safūd*) is an iron rod on which meat is roasted. The *shurb* (with a fatha) is a group of people drinking. The *mufta'ad* is the place of the fire where it is roasted. The line is from the Mu'allaqa of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī.]

That is, they abandoned it. And if it were from forgetting, they would have acted upon it once. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "*Nasītum* means you abandoned My command." Yaḥyā ibn Salām said: "It means you abandoned belief in the resurrection on this day." "*Nasīnākum*" means "We abandon you from good," as said by al-Suddī. Mujāhid said: "We abandon you in the punishment." In the resumption of His saying, "Indeed, We have forgotten you," and in the construction of the verb upon *inna* with its noun, there is emphasis on taking vengeance upon them. The meaning is: taste this, that is, what you are in of lowered heads, humiliation, and grief because of forgetting Allah. Or: taste the everlasting punishment, which is the lasting one with no cessation in Hell.

(﴿...for what you used to do﴾) means, in the world, of sins. The word "taste" may be used for what befalls the soul even if it is not eaten, since the soul perceives it as it perceives the taste of food. 'Umar ibn Abī Rabī'a said:

*So taste its abandonment, if you claim that it is corruption. Ah, how often the claim has lied!*

Al-Jawharī said: "*Dhuqtu mā 'inda fulān*" means I tested what he has, that is, I learned his condition. "*Dhuqtu al-qaws*" means when you pull its string to see how tight it is. "*Adhāqahu Allāh wabāla amrih*" means Allah made him taste the evil consequence of his affair. Ṭufayl said:

*So taste as we tasted on the morning of the ... from anger in our livers and grief.*

"*Tadhawwaqtahu*" means you tasted it little by little. "*Amrun mustadhaq*" means a matter that is tested and known. The poet said:

*The covenant of the fair ones is like the covenant of a smith, whose tools have grown slack from it, tested.*

And *al-dhawwāq* means one who quickly tires of things.

This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ): that they, because of their attachment to disbelief, do not believe in you. Rather, only those who ponder the Qur'an and are admonished by it believe in you and in the Qur'an. They are those who, when the Qur'an is recited to them, "fall down prostrating" (kharrū sujjadan). Ibn 'Abbas said: bowing (rukka'an). Al-Mahdawi said: this is according to the view of those who hold that one bows when reciting a prostration verse, and he cited the words of the Blessed and Exalted: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. And it has been said: what is meant is prostration, and most scholars hold this view, meaning they fell down prostrating to Allah the Exalted upon their faces, magnifying His signs and fearing His might and His punishment.

(And they glorify the praise of their Lord) meaning they combined glorification (tasbih) with praise (hamd), that is, they declared Him free of imperfection and praised Him, so they said in their prostration: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," "Glory be to my Lord the Most High and praise be to Him," meaning a declaration of Allah the Exalted's transcendence above the statement of the polytheists. Sufyan said: "And glorify the praise of their Lord" means they prayed, praising their Lord.

(And they are not proud) in worshipping Him; this was said by Yahya ibn Sallam. An-Naqqash: "They are not proud" as the people of Makkah were proud and refused to prostrate.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾, meaning they rise and withdraw from the places of lying down. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "their sides forsaking the beds." Al-madaji' is the plural of madja', which is the place of sleep. It is possible that ʿan here means "at the time of lying down," but that is a figurative usage (majaz), and the literal meaning (haqiqa) is preferable. From this is the saying of ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah:

*And among us is the Messenger of Allah, who recites his Book*
*When a light of dawn bursts forth, shining from the morning.*

*He spends the night, his side withdrawn from his bedding,*
*When the beds are heavy with the polytheists.*

Al-Zajjaj and al-Rummani said: *al-tajafi* is withdrawing to a higher direction. It is likewise used for pardoning one who wrongs you by insult or the like. *Al-junub* is the plural of *janb*. Regarding the reason for which their sides forsake their beds, there are two opinions:

The first: it is for the remembrance of Allah, either in prayer or outside prayer. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

The second: it is for prayer. Regarding the prayer for which their sides forsake their beds, there are four opinions:

The first: voluntary prayer (tanafful) at night. This was said by the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun), and most people hold it. It is the one in which praise lies, and it is the view of Mujahid, al-Awza'i, Malik ibn Anas, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Abu al-Aliyah and others. The Almighty's words support it: ﴿So no soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17], because they are rewarded for what they concealed with what is concealed. And Allah knows best. Its explanation will come later. There are many reports about night prayer (qiyam al-layl). Among them is the hadith of Muʿadh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Shall I not guide you to the gates of good? Fasting is a shield, charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire, and a man's prayer in the depth of the night." He said: then he recited: "Their sides forsake their beds," until he reached "they used to do." (Related by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in his Musnad, al-Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq, and Abu ʿIsa al-Tirmidhi, who said of it: a hadith that is hasan sahih.)

The second: the ʿIsha' prayer, which is called al-ʿAtamah. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAta'. In al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, it is reported that this verse, "Their sides forsake their beds," was revealed concerning waiting for the prayer called al-ʿAtamah. He said: this is a hasan gharib hadith.

The third: voluntary prayer between Maghrib and ʿIsha'. This was said by Qatadah and ʿIkrimah. Abu Dawud related on the authority of Anas ibn Malik that this verse, "Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and hope, and from what We have provided them they spend," was [revealed about people who] would perform voluntary prayers between Maghrib and ʿIsha'.

The fourth: al-Dahhak said: the withdrawal of the side is that a man prays ʿIsha' and Subh in congregation. This was also said by Abu al-Darda' and ʿUbadah.

I say: this is a good opinion, and it gathers the opinions in meaning. That is because the one who waits for ʿIsha' until he prays it is in prayer and in remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man remains in prayer as long as he awaits the prayer." Anas said: the intended meaning of the verse is waiting for the late ʿIsha' prayer, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to delay it until about a third of the night. Ibn ʿAtiyah said: the people of the Jahiliyyah used to sleep from the first of sunset and at whatever time a person wished, so waiting for the time of ʿIsha' came as something strange and burdensome. And one who prays Subh in congregation, especially at the beginning of its time, as the Prophet (peace be upon him) used to pray it, the custom is that whoever maintains this prayer at the beginning of its time rises at dawn, performs ablution and prays, and remembers Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, until the dawn rises. Thus withdrawal has been achieved at the beginning of the night and at its end. This is reinforced by what Muslim related from the hadith of Uthman ibn ʿAffan, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever prays ʿIsha' in congregation, it is as if he stood for half the night, and whoever prays Subh in congregation, it is as if he stood the whole night." The wording of al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud in this hadith is: "Whoever attends ʿIsha' in congregation, he has the reward of standing for half a night, and whoever prays ʿIsha' and Fajr in congregation, he has the reward of standing a whole night." It has already passed in Surah al-Nur, from Ka'b, concerning the one who prays four rak'ahs after the late ʿIsha' prayer that they will be for him equal to the Night of Decree [[See vol. 12, p. 308.]]. Fine reports have come concerning the virtue of prayer between Maghrib and ʿIsha' and of night prayer. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Yahya ibn Ayyub told us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj, or Ibn Abi al-Hajjaj, told me that he heard ʿAbd al-Karim narrate that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever performs ten rak'ahs between Maghrib and ʿIsha', a palace will be built for him in Paradise." ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said to him: "Then our palaces and houses will multiply, O Messenger of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is greater and better" — or he said: "more pure."

From ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, he said: the prayer of the penitent (al-awwabin) is the seclusion between Maghrib and ʿIsha' until the people return to prayer. ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud used to pray at that hour and would say: "The prayer of heedlessness is between Maghrib and ʿIsha'." Ibn al-Mubarak related it.

Al-Tha'labi related it with a marfu' chain from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever his two sides are withdrawn from the beds between Maghrib and ʿIsha', two palaces will be built for him in Paradise, a year's journey in extent, and in them are trees such that if the people of the East and the West were to dwell in them, they would be sufficed in fruit." This is the prayer of the penitent and the heedlessness of the heedless. Indeed, among the accepted supplications that are not rejected is supplication between Maghrib and ʿIsha'.

A section on the virtue of withdrawal. Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: when the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: "You will know today who are the people of generosity. Let those who praise Allah in every state stand up." They will stand and be sent off to Paradise. Then he will call a second time: "You will know today who are the people of generosity. Let those whose sides used to withdraw from the beds stand up, 'calling upon their Lord in fear and hope, and from what We have provided them they spend.'" He said: they will stand and be sent off to Paradise. He said: then he will call a third time: "You will know today who are the people of generosity. Let those who were ﴿not diverted by trade or sale from the remembrance of Allah and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah, fearing a Day in which hearts and eyes will be overturned﴾ [al-Nur: 37] stand up," and they will stand and be sent off to Paradise.

Al-Tha'labi related it with a marfu' chain from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah gathers the first and the last on the Day of Resurrection, a caller will come and call out with a voice that all creation hears: 'The people of the gathering will know today who is more worthy of generosity. Let those whose sides used to withdraw from the beds stand up.' They will stand, and they will be few. Then he will call a second time: 'You will know today who is more worthy of generosity. Let those whom trade and sale do not divert from the remembrance of Allah stand up,' and they will stand. Then he will call a third time: 'You will know today who is more worthy of generosity. Let those who praise Allah in every state, in ease and in hardship, stand up,' and they will stand, and they will be few, and they will all be sent off to Paradise. Then the rest of the people will be called to account."

Ibn al-Mubarak also mentioned: Ma'mar informed us, from a man, from Abu al-ʿAla' ibn al-Shikhkhir, from Abu Dharr, who said: "Three are those at whom Allah laughs and in whom Allah rejoices: a man who rose at night and left his bed and his warmth, then performed ablution, doing it well, then stood to pray. Allah says to His angels: 'What moved My servant to do what he did?' They say: 'Our Lord, You know best.' He says: 'I know, but tell Me.' They say: 'He hoped for what You promised him and feared what You warned him of.' He says: 'I call you to witness that I have granted him security from what he feared and have made obligatory for him what he hoped for.'" He said: and a man who was in a expedition, met the enemy, his companions fled, but he stood firm until he was killed or Allah granted victory over them; Allah says to His angels the like of this account. And a man who traveled through a night until, at the end of the night, he and his companions halted; his companions slept while he stood to pray; Allah says to His angels ...

(And he mentioned the account.)

The Almighty's words: ﴿calling upon their Lord﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning "calling." It may also be a separate descriptive clause, meaning: their sides forsake their beds, and they too, in every state, call upon their Lord by night and by day. "Khawfan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and it may be a verbal noun. "Tama'an" is like it, meaning: fear of punishment and hope for reward. "Wa-mimma razaqnahum yunfiqun": "ma" may mean "that which" or be a verbal noun (masdariyyah), and in both cases it must be separated from "min" [the preposition]. [Note: the text found in the books of grammatical dictation states that it is permitted.] "Yunfiqun" — it was said: its meaning is the obligatory zakah. It was also said: the voluntary charities; and this latter view is more laudatory.

Hamzah recited "مَا أُخْفِيَ لَهُمْ" (*mā ukhfiya lahum*, "what has been concealed for them") with the *yā'* (ي) sukun (silent). The rest of the readers recited it with a *fatḥah* on the *yā'*. In the recitation (*qirā'ah*) of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "مَا نُخْفِي" (*mā nukhfī*, "what We conceal") with a *nūn* and a *ḍammah*. Al-Mufaddal transmitted from al-A'mash "مَا يُخْفَى لَهُمْ" (*mā yukhfā lahum*) with a *yā'* that has a *ḍammah* and an *fā'* that has a *fatḥah*. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah recited "مِنْ قُرَّاتِ أَعْيُنٍ" (*min qurrāti a'yun*, "of comforts for the eyes").

As for one who read the *yā'* of "مَا أُخْفِيَ" with sukun, the verb is in the imperfect (*mustaqbal*, future/present tense), and its *alif* is the *alif* of the first-person speaker. The "مَا" (*mā*) is in the accusative position, governed by "أُخْفِيَ" (*ukhfī*), and it is an interrogative (*istifhām*). The clause is in the accusative position, since it stands in the place of the two objects. The pronoun referring back to "مَا" is omitted.

As for one who read the *yā'* with a *fatḥah*, the verb is a past tense verb built for the passive voice (*fi'l māḍin mabnīy lil-maf'ūl*, a verb in the past tense with a passive form). The "مَا" is in the nominative position as the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic), and the predicate (*khabar*) is "أُخْفِيَ" together with what follows it. The pronoun in "أُخْفِيَ" refers back to "مَا".

Al-Zajjaj said: It is also read "مَا أَخْفَى لَهُمْ" (*mā akhfā lahum*), meaning "what God has concealed for them." This is the recitation of Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and the "مَا" is in the accusative position.

Al-Mahdawi said: As for one who recited "قُرَّاتِ أَعْيُنٍ", it is the plural of "قُرَّةٍ" (*qurrah*, comfort). The plural is acceptable here because it is attached to a plural noun. The singular is used because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and it functions as a noun of genus (*ism lil-jins*).

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: This does not contradict the written copy of the Qur'an (*muṣḥaf*), because the *tā'* of "قُرَّةِ" is written as a *tā'* according to the dialect of those who pronounce the connected form as if it were a pause, just as they wrote "رَحْمَتَ اللَّهِ" (*raḥmata Llāh*, "the mercy of God") with a *tā'*. It is not unusual for the *alif* to be dropped in the orthography of "قُرَّاتِ", although it is present in pronunciation, just as the dropping of the *alif* in "السَّمَاوَاتِ" (*al-samāwāt*, "the heavens") is not considered strange, although it is firmly present in speech and pronunciation. [[In some manuscripts: "al-muslimāt."]]

The intended meaning is that God, exalted is He, informed of the bounty that they will have, which no soul, no human, and no angel has known.

Regarding the meaning of this verse, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.'" Then he recited this verse: "Their sides forsake their beds..." up to His words: "as a reward for what they used to do." (Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Ṣaḥīḥ, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi.)

Ibn Mas'ud said: "In the Torah it is written: 'For those whose sides forsake their beds, there is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.'"

Ibn Abbas said: "The matter of this is greater and more magnificent than that its interpretation can be known."

I say: This honour is only for the people of the highest rank in Paradise, as is clarified in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, who traced it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "Moses (peace be upon him) asked his Lord: 'O Lord, who is the lowest in rank among the people of Paradise?' He said: 'He is a man who comes after the people of Paradise have entered Paradise. It will be said to him: "Enter Paradise." He will say: "O Lord, how, when the people have taken their places and claimed their shares?" It will be said to him: "Are you pleased that you have the like of the kingdom of one of the kings of the world?" He will say: "I am pleased, my Lord." He will be told: "For you is that, and the like of it, and the like of it, and the like of it, and the like of it." In the fifth he will say: "I am pleased, my Lord." It will be said: "This is for you, and ten times its like, and for you is what your soul desires and what your eye delights in." He will say: "I am pleased, my Lord." Moses said: "O Lord, then who is highest in rank?" He said: "Those whom I willed (*aradtu*, I chose), I planted (*gharastu*) their honour with My hand, and I sealed it, so no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to any human heart."'"

Al-Nawawi said: "As for *aradtu* ('I willed'), it is with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, and its meaning is 'I chose and selected.' As for *gharastu karāmatahum bi-yadī* ('I planted their honour with My hand'), its meaning is 'I selected them and took charge of them, so their honour is not open to change.'"

And Muslim also transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, blessed and exalted, says: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived, as a treasure, *bal*' (far beyond) what I have shown you.'" Then he recited: "No soul knows what has been concealed for them of comfort for the eyes." [[*Bal*: one of the words that function as verbs and is built on a *fatḥah*, like *kayfa* ('how'). Its meaning is: 'Set aside what I have shown you, for what has not been shown to you is greater,' as if he turned away from it, considering it small in comparison with what has not been revealed.' (Sharḥ al-Nawawi.)]]

Ibn Sirin said: What is meant by it is looking at God, exalted is He.

Al-Hasan said: The people concealed their deeds, so God, exalted is He, concealed for them what no eye has seen and no ear has heard.

There are three issues in this verse.

The first: God's words, "Is one who is a believer like one who is a defiant sinner? They are not equal" (﴿أَفَمَنْ كانَ مُؤْمِناً كَمَنْ كانَ فاسِقاً لَا يَسْتَوُونَ﴾). That is, the believer is not like the defiant sinner, and therefore We granted those believers a great reward. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' ibn Yasar said: the verse was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, because the two of them had a dispute (mulahah, meaning argument and quarrelling). Al-Walid said to him: "I am more eloquent of tongue than you, sharper of spear, and fuller of body in the battle-line" (وارد للكتيبة, and another report reads وأملى فِي الْكَتِيبَةِ). 'Ali said to him: "Be silent! For you are a defiant sinner (fasiq)," and so the verse was revealed. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas mention that it was revealed concerning 'Ali and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Ibn 'Atiyya said: according to this view, the verse must be Meccan, because 'Uqba was not in Medina; he was killed on the road to Mecca when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from Badr. The other report is challenged by the application of the name fisq (defiance) to al-Walid. This may be understood as referring to the early period of al-Walid's Islam, because of something in himself, or because of what is reported of his conveying false reports about the Banu al-Mustaliq, until the verse was revealed about him: ﴿إِنْ جاءَكُمْ فاسِقٌ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوا﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6] ("If a defiant sinner comes to you with a report, verify it"), as its explanation will come in Surat al-Hujurat (see vol. 16, p. 311). It may also be that the Sharia applies that term to him, because he was on the verge of what is transgressive. He is the one who drank wine in the time of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and led the people in the dawn prayer, then turned and said: "Do you want me to add more?" and similar things whose mention would be lengthy.

The second: When Allah the Exalted divided the believers and the defiant sinners, whom He called defiant because of disbelief (since the denial at the end of the verse requires this), this necessitated denying equality between the believer and the disbeliever. For this reason, retaliation (qisas) is not applied between them, since one of the conditions for retaliation to be obligatory is equality between the killer and the killed. Our scholars used this argument against Abu Hanifa regarding his view on a Muslim killing a dhimmi. He said: "He intended the denial of equality here in the Hereafter, in reward, and in this world, in justice (adala)." We have taken it in its general sense, and this is more sound, since there is no evidence specifying it. So said Ibn al-'Arabi.

The third: God's words, ﴿لَا يَسْتَوُونَ﴾ ("they are not equal"). Al-Zajjaj and others said: "man" (مَنْ) may apply to the singular and the plural. Al-Nahhas said: the word "man" conveys the sense of a group, which is why it says "they are not equal" (لَا يَسْتَوُونَ). This is the view of many grammarians. Some of them said: "they are not equal" is used for two persons, because two is a plural, since it is one joined with another. Al-Zajjaj also said this. The hadith supports this view, since it is from Ibn 'Abbas and others, who said: "Afaman kana mu'minan" was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and "kaman kana fasiqan" concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.

The poet said:

أَلَيْسَ الْمَوْتُ بَيْنَهُمَا سَوَاءً ... إِذَا مَاتُوا وَصَارُوا في القبور

"Is not death between them equal, when they die and are placed in the graves?"

The Exalted's saying: ﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, they will have the Gardens of Refuge (jannat al-ma'wa) as their dwelling﴾. He informed of the abode of the two groups tomorrow. So for the believers are the gardens of refuge, or they take refuge in the gardens. He added "the gardens" to "the refuge" because that place contains gardens.

"Nuzulan" means as hospitality. Nuzul (provision prepared for a guest) is what is readied for the one who lodges and the guest. It has already been discussed at the end of Surah Al 'Imran [See vol. 4, p. 321]. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the gardens," meaning that the gardens are prepared for them. It may also be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

(And as for those who defied) meaning they departed from faith into disbelief (fa-ma'wahumu al-nar), meaning their dwelling is therein.

(Whenever they wish to get out of it, they will be returned into it.) Meaning, when the blaze of the Fire pushes them up to its top, they are returned to their place in it, because they hope to get out of it. This has already been discussed in Surah al-Hajj [See vol. 12, p. 27].

(And it will be said to them) meaning the guardians of Hell say to them, or Allah says to them: (Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny.) Dhawq (tasting) is used both in the sense of physical sensation and in the figurative sense. Its explanation has already been given in this surah [See pp. 98 and 99 of this part].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely make them taste the lesser punishment﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Dahhak, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: the lesser punishment is the calamities of this world and its illnesses, with which the servants are tested until they repent. Ibn 'Abbas also said this. And it is also reported from him that it refers to the prescribed punishments (hudud). Ibn Mas'ud, al-Husayn ibn 'Ali and 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith said: it is killing by the sword on the day of Badr. Muqatil said: it is the hunger of seven years in Makkah, until they ate carrion. Mujahid also said this. And it is also reported from him: the lesser punishment is the punishment of the grave, and al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said this. They said: and the greater is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Qushayri said: it has also been said that it is the punishment of the grave. But this is open to question, because of His saying: "so that they may return." He said: whoever understands the punishment as killing, says: "so that they may return" means that those among them who remain may return.

There is no disagreement that the greater punishment is the punishment of Hell, except what is reported from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, that it is the emergence of the Mahdi with the sword. And the lesser (punishment) is the rising of prices. It has also been said that the meaning of His saying "so that they may return," according to the view of Mujahid and al-Bara', is: that they may desire to return and seek it, like His saying: ﴿So let us return, that we may do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12].[[See p. 95 of this part.]] The desire to return has been called a return, just as the desire to stand has been called standing, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you rise up to the prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].[[See vol. 6 p. 80 onward.]] And the reading of one who reads "yurja'un" (in the passive voice) supports this, as mentioned by al-Zamakhshari.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ meaning: there is no one more unjust to himself.

(than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord) meaning: of His proofs and indications.

(then turns away from them) by refusing to accept them.

(Indeed, We will take retribution upon the criminals) for their denial and their turning away.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 23–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, so do not be in doubt about meeting him﴾, i.e., do not be in doubt, O Muhammad, about meeting Moses. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and he met him on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). Qatadah said: the meaning is, "do not be in doubt that you met him on the night of the Isra'." The meaning is one and the same. It was also said: "do not be in doubt about meeting Moses on the Day of Resurrection, for you will meet him therein." It was also said: "do not be in doubt about Moses' receiving the Book with acceptance," as said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. And it is reported from al-Hasan that he said regarding its meaning: "And We certainly gave Moses the Book," but he was harmed and denied, so "do not be in doubt that he [i.e., you] will meet what he met of denial and harm." The pronoun is then referring to an omitted noun, and the meaning is "of meeting what he met." Al-Nahhas said: this is a strange opinion, though it comes from the narration of 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. It was also said that there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "Say, the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you (yatawaffakum), so do not be in doubt about meeting him," and so it came as a parenthetical interjection between "And We certainly gave Moses the Book" and "and We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel." The pronoun in "and We made it" has two possibilities: first, "We made Moses," as said by Qatadah; second, "We made the Book," as said by al-Hasan.

﴿And We made from among them imams﴾, i.e., leaders and exemplars who are followed in their religion. The Kufans read "a'immah" [with a hamzah on the first and second letters]. Al-Nahhas said: this is a grave error (lahn) according to all the grammarians, because it combines two hamzahs in a single word, and this is a subtle point of grammar. Its explanation: the original form is "a'immah," then the vowel of the mim was transferred to the hamzah and the mim was assimilated, and the second hamzah was softened so that two hamzahs would not come together. Combining two hamzahs in two separate syllables is unusual; but within a single syllable, it is not permitted except by softening the second, as in your saying "Adam" and "akhar." It is said: "hadha awamm min hadha wa-ayamm," with the waw and the ya'. This has already been discussed in [the commentary on] "Bara'ah" [[see vol. 8, p. 84 onward]]. And God the Exalted knows best. "Guiding by Our command," i.e., they call creation to Our obedience. "By Our command," i.e., We commanded them to that. It was also said: "by Our command" means "for Our command," i.e., they guide people to Our religion. Then it was said: the intended are the prophets, peace be upon them, as said by Qatadah. And it was said: the intended are the jurists and scholars.

﴿When they were patient﴾. The recitation of the common readers is "lamma" with a fatha on the lam and a shaddah on the mim, with fatha, meaning "when they were patient." Yahya, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited "limа sabaru" [with a kasra on the lam], meaning "due to their patience We made them imams." Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, considering the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, "bima sabaru" with the ba'. This patience is patience upon the religion and upon trials. It was also said: they were patient regarding the world.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., He will decide and judge between the believers and the disbelievers, rewarding each according to what he deserves. It was also said: He will judge between the prophets and their peoples, as related by al-Naqqash.

This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and he met him on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). Qatadah said: the meaning is, "do not be in doubt that you met him on the night of the Isra'." The pronoun in "and We made it" has two possibilities: first, "We made Moses," as said by Qatadah; second, "We made the Book," as said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 26:

Allah's words: ﴿Does it not guide them?﴾ Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Qatadah, and Abu Zayd, on the authority of Ya'qub, read "nahdi lahum" with a nun (we guide them). This is a clear reading. Al-Nahhas said: The reading with a ya' (yahdi) has a difficulty, because it is said that a verb cannot be without a subject, so where is the subject of "yahdi"? The grammarians discussed this. Al-Farra' said: "kam" (how many) is in the nominative position with "yahdi." This contradicts the principles of the grammarians, who state that the interrogative does not govern what precedes it, nor does what precedes it govern "kam" in any way, meaning what comes before it. The view of Abu al-'Abbas (al-Mubarrad) is that "yahdi" indicates guidance (al-huda), and the meaning is: "Has guidance not been made clear to them?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "Has Allah not guided them?", so the meaning of the ya' and the nun is one and the same, that is: "Have We not made clear to them Our destruction of the disbelieving generations before them?" Al-Zajjaj said: "kam" is in the accusative position with "ahlakna" (We destroyed). "Yamshuna fi masakinihim" (they walk in their dwellings): the pronoun in "yamshuna" may refer to those who walk in the dwellings of the destroyed, meaning: these people walk about and do not take heed. It may also refer to the destroyed, in which case it is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: "We destroyed them while they were walking in their dwellings."

(Verily in that are signs. Will they not hear?) The signs of Allah and His admonitions, so that they may be admonished.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that We drive the water to the barren land?﴾ That is, "Have they not known the perfection of Our power by Our driving the water to the dry land in which there is no vegetation, so that We may give it life?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Juruz is the land whose vegetation has been cut off (jurija, i.e., quti'a), either because of lack of water or because it has been grazed and its growth removed. It is not said of land that does not produce, such as salt-marsh (sibakh), that it is juruz. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that We bring forth thereby crops﴾.

Ibn Abbas said: it is a land in Yemen. Mujahid said: it is Abyan. Ikrimah said: it is the thirsty land (al-ardh al-zam'a). al-Dahhak said: it is the dead, thirsty land. al-Farra' said: it is the land in which there is no vegetation. al-Asma'i said: it is the land that produces nothing at all. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: it is unlikely that it refers to a specific land, because of the entry of the alif and lam (the definite article), although it would be permissible according to the view of one who says: al-Abbas and al-Dahhak. The chain of narration from Ibn Abbas is sound, with no flaw in it. This is only a descriptive epithet (na't), and an epithet for a definite noun takes the alif and lam. It is derived from their saying: "a rajul jarur" when he leaves nothing without eating it. The reciter (al-rajiz) said:

A cunning, greedy man, who weeps when he is hungry, and eats the dates without spitting out the stones.

Likewise, "a female camel jarur" is one that eats everything it finds. And "a jurra' sword" means a cutting, sharp sword. "Jarazat al-jarad al-zar'a" means the locusts uprooted the crop by eating it. al-Farra' and others related that it is said: ardh jurz, and juruz, and jarz, and jarazon (the four forms), with four dialectal variants, like bukhl, raghab, and rahab (in all four, four variants).

It has been narrated that this land has no rivers, is far from the sea, and that only rain-water (wid'an, i.e., moisture) reaches it each year, so they sow three times in every year. It is also narrated from Mujahid that it is the land of the Nile.

﴿So that We bring forth thereby crops﴾, that is, by the water. ﴿of which their cattle eat﴾, of the herbage and grass. ﴿and themselves﴾, of the grain, greens and fruits. ﴿Will they not then see?﴾ That is, will they know that We are able to restore them?

The phrase ﴿fa-nukhriju﴾ may be coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "nasuqu," or it may be a separate clause (munqati'an) from what precedes it. The phrase ﴿ta'kulu minhu an'amuhum﴾ is in the accusative position as a descriptive epithet (na't).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 32, verses 28–29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "When will this conquest be, if you are truthful?"﴾ "Matā" (when) is in the place of nominative case (marfu'), and it is permissible for it to be in the place of accusative case (nasb) as an adverb of time (zarf). Qatadah said: "al-Fath" means the judgment (al-qada'). Al-Farra' and al-Qutabi said: it means the conquest of Makkah. But more preferable than this is what Mujahid said: he said, it means the Day of Resurrection. It is narrated that the believers said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, will judge between us on the Day of Resurrection, so He will reward the good-doer and punish the wrongdoer." The disbelievers then said, mockingly: "When is the Day of the Conquest?", meaning this judgment. It is said that a judge is called "fatih" and "fattah," because things are opened (tanfatih) and resolved at his hands and separated. And in the Qur'an: ﴿Our Lord, decide (iftah) between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], and this has passed in al-Baqarah [vol. 2, p. 3 ff.] and elsewhere.

﴿Say: "On the Day of Conquest, faith will not benefit those who disbelieved, nor will they be reprieved."﴾ "On the Day of Conquest" is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Al-Farra' permitted the nominative. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be delayed or given respite for repentance, whether the Day of Conquest is the Day of Badr or the conquest of Makkah. At Badr they were killed, and on the day of the conquest they fled [in manuscript Sh: "were defeated"], and Khalid ibn al-Walid caught up with them and killed them.

**[Qur'an 32:30]** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So turn away from them﴾. It has been said: its meaning is, turn away from their folly and do not answer them except with what you have been commanded.

(And wait, for they too are waiting) That is, wait for the Day of the Conquest (al-Fath), the day when Allah judges in your favour over them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿So turn away from them﴾" means from the polytheists of Quraysh in Makkah, and that this is abrogated (naskh) by the sword in "Bara'ah" (Surat al-Tawbah), in His saying: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].[[See vol. 7, p. 72.]] "And wait" means my promise to you. It has been said: this refers to the Day of Badr. "For they too are waiting" means they wait for the calamities of time (ḥawādith al-zamān) to befall you. It has also been said: the verse is not abrogated, since turning away may occur alongside a command to fight, as in a truce (hudnah) and other cases. It has also been said: turn away from them after you have conveyed the proof, and wait, for they too are waiting.

If it is asked: how can they wait for the Resurrection while they do not believe in it? There are two answers to this. The first is that the meaning is that they await death, which is among the signs of the Resurrection, and so this is metaphorical (majāz). The second is that among them are those who doubt and among them are those who believe in the Resurrection, so this is an answer addressed to these two groups. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Sumayqa' recited: "innahum muntaẓirūn" with a fatḥah on the ẓā' (muntaẓarūn). It is also related from Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin. Al-Farra' said: this is not valid except with an ellipsis (iḍmār), its sense being: they are awaited (muntaẓarūn bihim), meaning they are the object of waiting. Abu Hatim said: the correct reading is with a kasrah, i.e. wait for their punishment, for they are waiting for your ruin (halākak). It has also been said that the reading of Ibn al-Sumayqa' (with a fatḥah on the ẓā') means: wait for their ruin, for they are deserving that their ruin be awaited, meaning that they are certainly going to perish; and wait for that, for the angels in heaven are waiting for it. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and it is the meaning of al-Farra's view. And Allah knows best.
